Abstract

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and the fastest-growing neurological condition globally, with an estimated 10.5 million people living with PD in 2026 and projections exceeding 14.2 million by 2040 according to the World Health Organization. Despite this staggering burden, diagnosis continues to depend on clinical motor signs that appear only after 60%–80% of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra have been irreversibly lost, and specialist misdiagnosis rates reach 25% at early disease stages even in dedicated movement disorder centers. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from 239 studies drawn from 5847 screened records (2016–2026), critically evaluating unimodal diagnostic approaches encompassing dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography (DAT-SPECT), quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), alpha-synuclein (α-syn) seed amplification assay (SAA), neurofilament light chain (NfL), genetic risk markers, voice and speech biomarkers, gait and movement metrics, electroencephalography (EEG), and handwriting analysis, alongside their integration into multimodal machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) frameworks with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) components. Across 87 quantitative studies, the α-syn SAA achieved a sensitivity of 84%–92% and specificity of 93%–98% in prodromal cohorts. DAT-SPECT achieved a pooled sensitivity and specificity of approximately 90% but could not differentiate PD from atypical parkinsonian syndromes (APS). Multimodal fusion architectures, particularly cross-attention transformers integrating motor, voice, and gait data, consistently outperformed unimodal approaches by 4%–8% in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with the largest gains in early stage detection and differential diagnosis tasks. XAI methods, including SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM), and integrated gradients, were reported in only 31% of deep learning studies. This indicates a transparency gap with direct regulatory consequences. Across all modalities, only 22% of studies reported external validation, and multicenter prospective evidence remains scarce. These two deficits, rather than model architecture, are now the principal barriers to clinical adoption. This review provides an actionable roadmap for researchers, clinicians, and regulatory agencies working in the PD diagnostics field.

1. Introduction

1.1. Background and epidemiology

Parkinson’s disease (PD) was first described systematically by James Parkinson in his 1817 monograph An Essay on the Shaking Palsy. It is the fastest-growing neurological disorder in the world. The Global Burden of Disease Study estimated that 10.5 million people live with PD in 2026, double the prevalence recorded in 1990 (G.B.D. 2021 Parkinson’s Disease Collaborators, 2024). In 2019, annual PD-related deaths exceeded 329,000, more than twice the 1990 figure (G.B.D. 2021 Parkinson’s Disease Collaborators, 2024, Dorsey et al., 2018). The World Health Organization (WHO) projects 12 million cases by 2030 and 14.2 million by 2040. Population aging, longer life expectancy in low-income settings, and exposure to pesticides and industrial solvents are the principal drivers (World Health Organization, 2023, Ascherio and Schwarzschild, 2016, Nandipati and Litvan, 2016).
In addition, the overall age-standardized death rate associated with PD has been increasing, from approximately 3.6 per 100,000 in 2016 to an estimated 5.6 per 100,000 in 2026. High-income countries tend to report numbers staying above 7 per 100,000, partly because diagnostic detection is more sensitive and partly because people can live longer after diagnosis when optimal treatment is available (G.B.D. 2021 Parkinson’s Disease Collaborators, 2024, Ou et al., 2021). This pattern comes up in Fig. 1, and it is shown pretty directly there. Regarding economics, the all-in yearly cost burden of PD in the United States alone is over $52 billion, meaning that it includes direct healthcare spending, unpaid family caregiving, and lost productivity. In other words, it has a similar order of magnitude and proportional weight as those reported elsewhere, such as across Western Europe and East Asia (Bloem et al., 2021, Armstrong and Okun, 2020).

1.2. Types and pathophysiology of Parkinson’s disease

PD is not a single uniform entity. At the pathological level, all clinically recognized forms share the hallmark of selective degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and the intraneuronal accumulation of misfolded alpha-synuclein (𝛼-syn) for Lewy bodies and neurites (Braak et al., 2003, Spillantini et al., 1997, Goedert et al., 2013). However, the genetic basis, rate of progression, pattern of spread, and relative contributions of dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic neurodegeneration differ substantially among individuals, justifying the conceptualization of PD as a heterogeneous syndrome rather than a single disease (Titova et al., 2017, Espay et al., 2017). Fig. 2 illustrates the major pathological and clinical subtypes of this disease.
The Braak staging hypothesis (Braak et al., 2003) proposes a stereotyped caudo-rostral progression of Lewy pathology beginning in the dorsal vagal nucleus and olfactory bulb (Stages 1–2), ascending to the SNpc and amygdala (Stages 3–4), and ultimately involving the neocortex (Stages 5 and 6). This staged progression provides a mechanistic explanation for the non-motor prodromal signs that appear before the classic motor symptoms begin, sometimes a decade or more later. There is also the “body-first vs. brain-first” model proposed by Borghammer and Van Den Berge (2019), which suggests that in some individuals, the pathology begins in the enteric nervous system and then gradually moves up toward the brain. In contrast, brain-first cases begin in the central nervous system, with earlier involvement of the substantia nigra. This division could also affect how we select biomarkers because the body-first group is more likely to show prodromal autonomic and sleep features, which are easier to detect early (Borghammer and Van Den Berge, 2019).
Clinical subtypes of PD are organized along two orthogonal axes. On the motor phenotype axis, tremor-dominant (TD) PD presents with a 4–6 Hz resting tremor, relatively preserved gait, and slower cognitive decline. The postural instability and gait difficulty (PIGD) subtype shows greater axial involvement, higher fall risk, and faster progression to dementia (Fereshtehnejad and Postuma, 2017). A mixed phenotype combining TD and PIGD features is common at later stages. On the etiological axis, idiopathic PD accounts for approximately 90% of cases and arises from gene-environment interactions (Wirdefeldt et al., 2011). Monogenic PD driven by pathogenic variants in SNCA (Polymeropoulos et al., 1997, Singleton et al., 2003), LRRK2 (leucine-rich repeat kinase 2) (Farrer, 2006), PRKN (parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase) (Kitada et al., 1998), PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1), and DJ-1 (Parkinsonism-associated deglycase) accounts for approximately 5%–10% of cases. Genetic-risk PD sits somewhere in between and connects to common risk variants, such as GBA1, MAPT, and SNCA non-coding polymorphisms (Blauwendraat et al., 2020, Nalls et al., 2019). In addition, the genetic basis of PD has been getting clearer, largely because of large genome-wide association studies (GWAS) with hundreds of thousands of participants, which have flagged more than 90 risk loci (Nalls et al., 2019). Finally, there are non-motor subtypes, such as PD with dementia, PD with autonomic failure, and PD with psychiatric presentations, which are often handled as separate clinical entities. Therefore, they need tailored management and additional diagnostic complications as part of the deal (Chaudhuri et al., 2006, Aarsland et al., 2021).

1.3. Why early diagnosis matters

The necessity for early diagnosis of PD is rooted in a number of competing and converging demands, which create clinical urgency. On the neuroprotection side, the best disease-modifying candidates being tested in the clinic right now, for example, of those mentioned above, a-syn immunotherapy, leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) kinase inhibitors, glucocerebrosidase B1 (GBA1)-directed enzyme replacement approaches, and mitochondrial cofactors, are thought to be most effective if applied prior to irreversible neuronal loss (Brundin et al., 2017b, Brundin et al., 2017a, Stocchi et al., 2024). However, in clinical practice, a confident clinical label can be difficult to assign before motor parkinsonism is well established (such that post-mortem studies demonstrate approximately 60%–80% SNpc neuronal loss at motor symptom onset Kalia and Lang, 2015, Dauer and Przedborski, 2003). In fact, this tightens the window for neuroprotection, frequently sealing it off before any intervention can be undertaken.
From a clinical standpoint, earlier diagnosis implies earlier initiation of dopaminergic replacement therapy, which results in symptomatic benefits throughout the disease course (Connolly and Lang, 2014, Rizek et al., 2016). It also facilitates earlier referral for speech therapy, physiotherapy, and occupational therapy, which enhances the quality of life and reduces caregiver burden if initiated prior to significant functional decline (Armstrong and Okun, 2020). Then, there is the economic aspect, which also rings true: misdiagnosis occurs in 15%–25% of patients, even at tertiary movement disorder centers (Rizzo et al., 2016). This error in diagnosis may result in unnecessary dopaminergic treatment in patients with essential tremor or drug-induced Parkinson’s disease, and it may also postpone appropriate management for those who are erroneously labeled as having something else. For trial design, reliable early diagnosis and/or correct subtype identification are fundamental if one wishes to enroll in disease-modifying trials that require biologically homogeneous patient cohorts (Berg et al., 2024, Simuni et al., 2020).
The prodromal stage of PD offers an opening that is becoming more accessible every year. Non-motor prodromal clues, such as REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), anosmia, constipation, and depression, may appear 10–20 years before motor onset (Berg et al., 2015, Ross et al., 2008, Iranzo et al., 2013). Individuals with isolated RBD can have a conversion chance of developing PD or a related synucleinopathy higher than 75% over 10 years (Iranzo et al., 2013). Spotting these individuals, grading their conversion probability, and beginning biological surveillance are the key aims of pushing the biomarker and ML efforts reviewed in this study. Fig. 3 shows the major motor and non-motor health complications associated with PD over the full disease trajectory.

1.4. Rationale for this review

Several reviews on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in PD have been published since 2020. Most of them focus on a single modality, most often voice or gait, and treat ML as an organizing concept. Four specific problems motivated the design of this study. First, we were unable to identify an existing review in which biofluid, genetic, imaging, and digital biomarkers were evaluated within a single quality-assessed framework. Because clinicians are required to select among these modalities in practice, a comparison conducted under a common evidential standard would be valuable. Second, the field has changed significantly since 2023. Alpha-synuclein SAA was validated in a 1123-participant cohort, a neuronal alpha-synuclein disease staging framework was proposed, and transformer-based fusion models were introduced. Reviews published before 2024 predate these advances and are therefore outdated and less relevant. Third, with the adoption of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (2024), explainability has arguably shifted from an academic preference to regulatory expectations. To the best of our knowledge, the frequency with which XAI has been reported in PD diagnosis studies has not been quantified. Fourth, published accuracy figures are frequently cited without reference to the validation strategy used to obtain them. Accordingly, the validation strategy was extracted for every included study, and the performance was reported separately for internally and externally validated models. This review addresses these four questions. It is intended to serve as a decision-support resource for researchers engaged in the design of diagnostic studies, clinicians interpreting biomarker evidence, and regulatory bodies appraising AI-based diagnostic submissions.

1.5. Evolution of PD diagnostics: A chronological perspective

The diagnostic approach to PD has passed through four overlapping eras, and understanding this sequence clarifies the current status of the field.
Clinical era (1817–2000). Diagnosis was based on expert observation of cardinal motor signs. The United Kingdom Brain Bank criteria and later the Movement Disorder Society (MDS) criteria formalized this process, but autopsy-confirmed accuracy remained near 80% (Hughes et al., 1992, Rizzo et al., 2016, Postuma et al., 2015).
Imaging era (2000–2015). Dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography (DAT-SPECT) provided the first objective in vivo measure of nigrostriatal integrity and received regulatory approval (Tolosa et al., 2006). Its limitation was recognized early: it detects dopaminergic denervation but cannot distinguish between PD and APS.
Machine learning era (2015–2022). Support vector machines and random forests were applied to voice, gait, and imaging features, with reported accuracies of 85%–95% (Tsanas et al., 2010, Little et al., 2009, Prashanth et al., 2016). Deep learning followed, removing the need for hand-crafted features (Tagaris et al., 2018). Most of this work used single-center data and internal cross-validation.
Biological and multimodal era (2022–present). Three developments define the current period. Alpha-synuclein SAA has established a molecular anchor for diagnosis (Kang et al., 2019, Berg et al., 2024). Multimodal fusion architectures have demonstrated consistent gains over single-modality models (Frontiers Research Team, 2025, Makarious et al., 2022). XAI methods have been applied to check model decisions against known neuropathology (Lundberg and Lee, 2017, Ren et al., 2025).
Collectively, these four eras suggest a progression from subjective clinical observation toward objective imaging, subsequently toward data-driven prediction, and more recently toward biologically anchored multimodal inference accompanied by transparency requirements. Nevertheless, the transition from retrospective single-center accuracy to prospective multicenter demonstration of clinical utility appears to remain incomplete. The conditions that such a transition would require are considered in Section 5.4.

1.6. Research gaps

Despite the substantial research effort reviewed here, five major gaps persist, which limit their clinical translation.
External validation deficit. Only 22% of the ML studies reviewed here reported external validation on a dataset that was independent of the training cohort, and this is important. A number of studies that directly compared internal cross-validation to external validation within the same work found a fairly consistent median performance drop of approximately 5%–8% in AUC. Therefore, in practice, the internally validated numbers are probably overestimates of real-world diagnostic accuracy by something like the same commensurate margin. This inflation is particularly pronounced for high-dimensional feature sets, where model overfitting to training The cohort-specific characteristics were the most severe.
Standardization absence. No consensus exists on recording equipment, task protocol, or signal preprocessing pipeline for digital biomarkers including voice (microphone type, room acoustics, phonation task duration), gait (IMU body placement, walking task, walking speed), or EEG (electrode montage, reference, and artifact removal). This absence makes cross-study comparisons unreliable and prevents meaningful Meta-analytic pooling of performance estimates.
Demographic bias and limited diversity. Approximately 61% of the included studies recruited participants exclusively from North America or Western Europe. GWAS discovery cohorts used to derive polygenic risk scores (PRS) are approximately 80% of European ancestry (Nalls et al., 2019, Blauwendraat et al., 2020), substantially limiting the accuracy of PRS-based risk stratification in East Asian, South Asian, African, and Latin American populations, where allele frequencies and linkage disequilibrium patterns differ markedly.
Prodromal cohort scarcity. Only 15% of included studies enrolled prodromal (pre-motor) participants, the population most clinically relevant for neuroprotective interventions. The scarcity of prodromal data reflects the logistical and financial challenges of recruiting and following large cohorts of asymptomatic at-risk individuals, respectively, over multiple years.
XAI underutilization. Explainability methods were reported in only 31% of the DL studies. Given that the European Union AI Act (2024) classifies AI-based medical diagnostics as high-risk systems requiring explainability documentation, and that the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance on AI/ML-based software as a medical device (SaMD) emphasizes transparency, this gap represents a direct barrier to regulatory approval of clinical diagnostic tools (Arrieta et al., 2020, U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2021).

1.7. Research questions

This systematic review addressed the following five research questions.
  • RQ1.
    What unimodal diagnostic biomarkers are available for PD and what is their evidence-based diagnostic performance across different disease stages and clinical tasks?
  • RQ2.
    Which ML and DL algorithms have been applied to PD diagnosis, and how do their performance characteristics compare across modalities, disease stages, and validation strategies?
  • RQ3.
    How does multimodal integration improve diagnostic accuracy compared with unimodal approaches, and which fusion strategies are most effective?
  • RQ4.
    What is the current state of XAI in PD diagnosis, and how do XAI methods support clinical trust and regulatory compliance?
  • RQ5.
    What are the principal barriers to clinical translation of AI-based PD diagnostic tools, and what research priorities would most effectively address them?

1.8. Research contributions

This review makes the following contributions.
  • 1.
    A quality-assessed synthesis of 239 studies covering nine unimodal modalities and four multimodal fusion architecture categories, structured according to PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021) and QUADAS-2 (Whiting et al., 2011) standards.
  • 2.
    A structured comparative analysis of ML, DL, and XAI methods across modalities and disease stages, including the first tabulation of XAI technique distribution across reviewed PD diagnostic studies.
  • 3.
    A novel comparative table contrasting this review against ten prior systematic reviews in scope, breadth, and methodological rigor, identifying specific advances made here.
  • 4.
    An integrated analysis of ethical, regulatory, and health equity considerations including an assessment of geographic and demographic bias in the training data used by reviewed studies.
  • 5.
    A structured research agenda addressing all five identified gaps, serving as a reference framework for future grant applications, trial design, and regulatory submissions.

1.9. Paper organization

Section 2 presents the systematic review methodology. Section 3 reports results organized by modality and analytical approach. Section 4 discusses the evidence, including XAI, clinical implications, comparison with Previous reviews and limitations. Section 5 provides conclusions and future directions.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Protocol, registration, and reporting standards

This review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021).
We applied PRISMA 2020 as the primary reporting standard because the review addressed a focused diagnostic accuracy question with pre-specified eligibility criteria and formal risk-of-bias assessment. We additionally drew on the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) for two elements only: the mapping of diagnostic modality domains (Fig. 4) and charting of evidence across heterogeneous study designs. These two elements are outside the scope of the standard PRISMA.Quality assessment was performed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool for primary diagnostic accuracy studies (Whiting et al., 2011) and A MeaSurement Tool to Assess systematic Reviews-2 (AMSTAR-2) for secondary reviews (Shea et al., 2017). Evidence synthesis follows the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) framework (Campbell et al., 2020) given the methodological heterogeneity of the included literature.
This review was not prospectively registered in the PROSPERO database. We acknowledge this limitation and report it transparently rather than claiming pending registration. To mitigate the associated risk of selective reporting, the protocol elements (search strings, eligibility criteria, data extraction fields, and quality assessment instruments) were fixed in writing before screening began, and no post-hoc changes were made to the eligibility criteria or outcome definitions.

2.2. Search strategy and Boolean strings

Five electronic databases were searched: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science (Core Collection), IEEE Xplore, and the Cochrane Library. All searches were conducted between January 6 and 17, 2026. The final search was conducted on January 24, 2026, to capture records added during the screening period. The publication window was from January 2016 to January 2026. The applied filters and limits were identical across databases where the interface permitted: language restricted to English, document type restricted to journal articles, reviews, and conference papers with full text, species filter set to human in PubMed, and no restriction on study design at the search stage. No filters were applied to the sample size, country, or funding sources.
Table 1 presents the complete Boolean string for each database, combining controlled vocabulary (Medical Subject Headings in PubMed and Emtree equivalents in Scopus) with free-text terms. Backward citation searching was performed on the reference lists of all the included systematic reviews, and forward citation searching was performed in Google Scholar for the ten most-cited included studies. Fig. 4 presents the hierarchical categorization of the diagnostic modality domains.

2.3. Study selection

All retrieved titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers against the pre-specified eligibility criteria. Full-text articles were retrieved for all records that satisfied the screening criteria. Disagreements between the two reviewers were resolved by a third party. The degree of concordance between the reviewers was quantified using Cohen’s kappa coefficient.
Inclusion criteria:
  • •
    Original research article, systematic review, or meta-analysis with quantitative synthesis
  • •
    Human participants with clinically diagnosed or suspected PD, prodromal PD, or healthy controls
  • •
    Any unimodal or multimodal diagnostic approach
  • •
    At least one performance metric reported: sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, or AUC
  • •
    English language
Exclusion criteria:
  • •
    Non-human or in-vitro studies
  • •
    Case reports or case series (𝑛<20 participants)
  • •
    Conference abstracts without associated peer-reviewed full text
  • •
    Studies focused on therapeutic monitoring or treatment response without diagnostic component
  • •
    Narrative reviews without quantitative synthesis
Justification of two eligibility decisions. Two aspects of the eligibility framework merit further explanation, as their rationale may not be evident.
Treatment of selected pre-2016 sources. Although the search window commenced in January 2016, a limited number of earlier publications are cited within the narrative sections of this review. These sources are exclusively definitional or foundational in character, and no superseding equivalents appear to be available; representative examples include the Braak staging scheme (Braak et al., 2003), the original descriptions of the SNCA and PRKN loci (Polymeropoulos et al., 1997, Kitada et al., 1998), and the MDS clinical diagnostic criteria (Postuma et al., 2015). Although such works provide necessary conceptual background, they contribute no diagnostic performance data. Accordingly, they were not counted among the 239 included studies, were not represented within the PRISMA flow diagram, and did not enter into any element of the quantitative synthesis. This distinction between narrative citation and evidential inclusion is made explicit here to avoid potential ambiguity.
Exclusion of studies enrolling fewer than 20 participants. This threshold was established a priori, and two considerations informed its selection. First, diagnostic accuracy estimates derived from very small samples are attended by confidence intervals of such width that they are unlikely to contribute meaningfully to comparative synthesis; where 𝑛<20, the 95% confidence interval surrounding a point sensitivity estimate of 90% would extend from approximately 68% to 99%. Second, machine learning models trained on fewer than 20 participants are widely acknowledged to be susceptible to overfitting, with the consequence that their reported accuracies may not be interpretable as indicators of generalizable performance. It should be noted that the threshold was applied to the number of participants rather than to the number of recordings or images; studies enrolling 20 or more participants, each contributing multiple samples, were therefore retained.

2.4. Data extraction and quality assessment

Data were extracted using a pre-specified spreadsheet capturing first author, year, country, study design, participant characteristics (sample size, age range, sex ratio, disease stage), index test, reference standard, ML or DL model, validation strategy, and all reported performance metrics with 95% confidence intervals (CI) where available. For multimodal studies, the modality combination and fusion architecture were recorded.
Extraction procedure and agreement. Two reviewers extracted data independently into duplicate spreadsheets. A pilot round on 20 randomly selected studies preceded full extraction, after which the extraction form was refined once. Agreement between reviewers was calculated on the pilot set and on a further 15% random sample of included studies. Cohen’s kappa was 0.86 for eligibility decisions and 0.81 for QUADAS-2 domain judgments, both in the substantial agreement range. Disagreements were settled by discussion, and a third reviewer arbitrated the 11 unresolved cases.
Risk-of-bias scoring. Quality assessment followed QUADAS-2 across four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing (Whiting et al., 2011). Each domain was rated low, high, or unclear risk using the signaling questions of the original instrument. A domain was rated high risk if any signaling question was answered “no,” unclear if information was insufficient, and low risk otherwise. Applicability concerns were recorded separately for the first three domains. No study was excluded on the basis of its risk-of-bias rating; instead, results from high-risk studies are flagged throughout and excluded from the sensitivity analysis described below.
Synthesis method. We did not perform meta-analytic pooling. The decision was made a priori and rested on the degree of clinical and methodological heterogeneity across included studies: reference standards differed (clinical diagnosis in 98% of studies, neuropathological confirmation in the remainder), index tests were non-comparable across modalities, and threshold selection for binary metrics was study-specific. Pooling under these conditions produced summary estimates that were statistically defensible but clinically uninterpretable. We therefore followed the SWiM reporting framework (Campbell et al., 2020) and synthesized the results as follows. Performance metrics are reported as medians with full ranges across studies, grouped by modality and validation strategy. Where three or more studies reported the same metric for the same modality and comparison, we additionally reported the interquartile range. The direction of effect for multimodal versus unimodal comparisons was assessed by counting the studies favoring each approach, using the best unimodal baseline reported within the same study as the comparator, which controls for between-study heterogeneity. Vote counting is reported alongside effect magnitudes and is not used as the sole basis for any conclusion. As a sensitivity analysis, all summary ranges were recalculated after excluding studies rated high risk of bias in two or more QUADAS-2 domains; the resulting shifts in median AUC were below 0.02 for every modality and did not alter the ranking of modalities.
Statistical reporting conventions. Throughout the Results, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy are given as percentages and AUC as a decimal fraction. Where the primary study reported 95% CI, these are reproduced. Where a study reported only a point estimate, this is stated. We do not compute or impute CI for studies that did not report them, and we do not report 𝑝-values for between-study comparisons, since the studies are not randomized against one another and such tests would be misleading. Table 2 presents the distribution of included studies by database and study type, while Table 3 presents the QUADAS-2 risk-of-bias summary.

3. Results

3.1. PRISMA flow and study characteristics

The PRISMA 2020 flow for this review is illustrated in Fig. 5. Database searches resulted in 5847 records; after removing 1234 duplicates, 4613 records underwent the title and abstract screening phase. Of these, 3094 studies were excluded because they were not relevant to PD diagnosis (1, 200; pre-2015 but non-foundational: 907; non-human: 95; other reasons: 892). Subsequently, full-text review was performed for 1519 records, and 1280 were excluded (sample size under 20:218; no performance metric provided: 412; conference abstract only: 95; narrative review without quantitative synthesis: 555). Finally, 239 studies satisfied all inclusion conditions and entered the qualitative synthesis, with 87 having sufficient numerical metrics for the head-to-head comparative analyses seen in the tables and figures that follow.
The 239 included studies were conducted in 38 countries. North America, along with Western Europe, contributed 61% of the studies, East Asia accounted for 22%, the Middle East for 9%, and the remaining regions for 8%. The sample sizes varied greatly from 20 to 156,000 (median 142). Approximately 47% of the studies enrolled only early stage PD participants, using Hoehn and Yahr Stages I–II; 38% had mixed disease stages, and 15% targeted prodromal cohorts. The spread of the study cohorts across geography is illustrated in Fig. 7 (see Fig. 6).

3.2. Evidence classes among included studies

The 239 included studies were not methodologically equivalent, and pooling them without distinction would obscure important differences in evidential weight. Therefore, we separated them into three classes and reported the findings by class throughout the Results section.
Class A: primary diagnostic accuracy studies (𝑛=172, 72.0%). This report presents the original diagnostic performance on a defined participant sample against a stated reference standard. These are the source of all model-level performance figures in Table 7, Table 8, Table 9, Table 10, Table 11. Of these, 134 (77.9%) used internal validation only, and 38 (22.1%) reported external validation on an independent dataset.
Class B: systematic reviews and meta-analyses (𝑛=41, 17.2%). These provide pooled estimates across primary studies. They were appraised with AMSTAR-2 (Shea et al., 2017): 9 were rated high confidence, 19 moderate, 11 low, and 2 critically low. We cite Class B evidence for pooled sensitivity and specificity figures (for example, the DAT-SPECT and NfL meta-analytic estimates), and we note the AMSTAR-2 rating where a figure is load-bearing for our conclusions. Primary study data were not double-counted with pooled estimates drawn from the same primary studies.
Class C: prospective and longitudinal validation studies (𝑛=21, 8.8%). These enrolled participants were prospectively followed over time, or a previously trained model was validated in a new cohort. This class carries the greatest weight for clinical translation and is the smallest. Only 6 of the 21 were multicenter. Only three evaluated a locked model, that is, one whose parameters were fixed before the validation data were seen. This scarcity is the single most consequential finding of this review with respect to clinical readiness, and Section 3.3 develops it.
A further five studies (2.1%) were secondary analyses of public datasets and are reported separately where relevant, since they share participants with other included studies and cannot be treated as independent evidence.

3.3. External validation, multicenter evidence, and prospective testing

Because model generalizability determines clinical usefulness, we extracted the validation strategy for every Class A study and analyzed the performance by validation type.
The internal-external performance gap. Among the 87 studies with fully extractable quantitative metrics, 19 (21.8%) reported both internal cross-validation and external validation of the same model. In these studies, the median AUC fell from 0.94 (range 0.88–0.98) under internal cross-validation to 0.87 (range 0.76–0.94) under external validation. The median within-study drop was 0.067 AUC, and the drop exceeded 0.05 in 13 of the 19 studies. The magnitude of the decline was largest for high-dimensional voice feature sets and smallest for biofluid assays, which is consistent with overfitting to site-specific recording conditions rather than genuine biological signal loss.
Implication for reported accuracy. Notably, this pattern does not appear to be unique to PD. Systematic appraisals conducted in other clinical domains have reported a comparable internal-to-external gap, along with a similar predominance of models that remain externally unvalidated (Wynants et al., 2020, Futoma et al., 2020, Ramspek et al., 2021). Given that 77.9% of Class A studies did not evaluate their model beyond the training cohort, the accuracy figures most frequently cited within the PD AI literature might most appropriately be interpreted as optimistic upper bounds. Applying the observed median drop of 0.067 to the internally validated median AUC of 0.91 yields an expected real-world AUC near 0.84 for a typical published model. This would represent a considerable divergence between reported and anticipated clinical performance, and it may plausibly account, at least in part, for the fact that no AI-based PD diagnostic tool has yet entered routine clinical practice.
Multicenter evidence. Only six of 239 studies (2.5%) were recruited from more than three centers. The PPMI cohort (Marek et al., 2011) accounts for a large share of the multicenter evidence base and is itself concentrated in North America and Western Europe. Site-level heterogeneity in scanner hardware, acquisition protocol, and clinical rating practice would therefore appear to be under-represented within the present literature, with the consequence that models are being trained upon data of lesser diversity than the populations within which their deployment is envisaged.
Prospective clinical trials. We identified no randomized trial in which an AI-based diagnostic tool was compared against standard clinical assessment with a patient-relevant endpoint. The three locked-model prospective studies were single-arm and reported diagnostic concordance rather than clinical benefit. However, diagnostic accuracy, however favorable, constitutes a surrogate for clinical utility; it does not in itself establish that the deployment of a given model alters clinical management or improves patient outcomes. In the absence of such trials, it would seem difficult to substantiate claims of clinical readiness on the basis of the evidence base examined here (Kelly et al., 2019).

3.4. Performance metrics used in model evaluation

Diagnostic performance reporting was heterogeneous across included studies. Table 4 presents the formal mathematical definitions of all metrics encountered in the review. Accuracy was the most commonly reported metric (93% of quantitative studies), while Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) and Cohen’s kappa, which are more robust under class imbalance, were reported in only 14% and 9% in the studies, respectively. Only 36% of studies reported 95% confidence intervals for their primary performance metric, limiting the interpretability of individual study results. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis with AUC was used in 77% of studies and is the preferred metric for cross-study comparison given its independence from the decision threshold and class prevalence.

3.5. Clinical diagnosis and staging

Clinical diagnosis of PD rests on the MDS clinical diagnostic criteria published in 2015 (Postuma et al., 2015), which require the presence of bradykinesia combined with resting tremor and/or rigidity as the core parkinsonis definition, supplemented by supportive criteria, absolute exclusion criteria, and red flags. The MDS-UPDRS (Goetz et al., 2008) quantifies motor and non-motor symptom severity across four subscales and is the principal outcome measure in virtually all reviewed clinical studies. The five-stage Hoehn and Yahr scale (Hoehn and Yahr, 1967) provides a coarser staging index widely used in clinical practice and trial enrollment. Even in dedicated movement disorder centers with highly experienced specialists, autopsy-confirmed accuracy is 80%–85% (Hughes et al., 1992, Rizzo et al., 2016), with the most common source of misdiagnosis being APS including multiple system atrophy (MSA), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) (Litvan et al., 1996), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) (McKeith et al., 2017), and corticobasal syndrome. Essential tremor (Bhidayasiri, 2005) and drug-induced parkinsonism account for a further proportion of misdiagnoses, particularly in primary care settings, where specialist input is limited. This diagnostic gap provides the primary motivation for the biomarker and the computational approaches reviewed in the following sections.

3.6. Unimodal diagnostic approaches

3.6.1. Neuroimaging

Dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography (DAT-SPECT) using the radioligand 123I-ioflupane (DaTSCAN, GE Healthcare) measures presynaptic dopaminergic terminal density by to reflect radiotracer binding in the striatum. In idiopathic PD, uptake is asymmetrically and preferentially reduced in the posterior putamen, progressing to global striatal involvement at an advanced stage. A meta-analysis encompassing 44 studies reported pooled sensitivity of 90% (95% CI 88%–92%) and specificity of 91% (95% CI 89%–93%) for distinguishing degenerative from non-degenerative parkinsonism (Tolosa et al., 2006, Prasuhn et al., 2021). This technique is FDA- and EMA-approved and has a supportive criterion status within the MDS diagnostic framework (Postuma et al., 2015). One limitation overlooked in the main studies is that DAT-SPECT cannot distinguish PD from APS, including MSA, PSP, and DLB, and these conditions show similar reductions in striatal tracer uptake (Rizzo et al., 2016). In addition, there is radiation exposure, and the per-scan price typically falls between $2500 to $4000. Access is limited by the availability of gamma cameras, particularly in low-income and middle-income countries (Bloem et al., 2021). On the other hand, 3D CNN-based automated categorization of DAT-SPECT data has shown sensitivity near 94% and specificity of about 91% in retrospective single-center studies (Tagaris et al., 2018, Nandakumar et al., 2021). More recently, residual network approaches have reported AUC scores above 0.95 when using multicenter datasets (Vu et al., 2023).
Positron emission tomography (PET) with 18F-fluorodopa measures presynaptic dopamine synthesis and offers superior spatial resolution compared with SPECT, with pooled sensitivity of 85%–96% and specificity of 85%–97% across multiple cohorts (Bhatt and Bhidayasiri, 2020, Meles et al., 2018). 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET reveals characteristic patterns of regional brain metabolism that are diagnostically distinct across PD and APS: frontoparietal and midbrain hypometabolism in PSP, olivopontocerebellar or striatal hypometabolism in MSA, and relatively preserved parieto-occipital metabolism in PD, enabling differential diagnosis with specificity exceeding 90% at tertiary centers (Bhatt and Bhidayasiri, 2020). Tau PET tracers have recently expanded the differential diagnostic toolkit, with 18F-GTP1 demonstrating visual binding to PSP-specific tau deposits that is diagnostically distinct from PD (Bhatt and Bhidayasiri, 2020). The principal barriers to PET adoption remain its substantial cost and the cyclotron infrastructure required for radiotracer production.
Advanced quantitative MRI attempts to solve the specificity limits seen in DAT-SPECT without bringing along the radiation burden; thus, it is more “gentle” for patients. Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) uses magnetization transfer contrast tied to neuromelanin-bound paramagnetic complexes, mainly in the SNpc and locus coeruleus. In practice, this leads to lower signal intensities in PD, which track neuronal loss, although not perfectly, but sufficiently to be useful. In one meta-analysis, 16 studies with 1047 participants gave a pooled sensitivity of 83% and specificity of 86% when compared to clinical PD diagnosis (Prasuhn et al., 2021). In addition, quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) looks for abnormal iron build-up in the SNpc, which is a stable hallmark of PD and can be paired with NM-MRI to push the overall ability to separate PD from controls even further. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) of nigrostriatal white matter tracts reveals microstructural changes in the posterior substantia nigra which distinguishes patients with PD from healthy controls (Vaillancourt et al., 2009). Free water imaging of the posterior substantia nigra, a more recent technique, has demonstrated specificity exceeding 85% for PD versus APS discrimination in prospective cohorts. A notable landmark in multi-contrast MRI-based classification comes from the combination of QSM and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) in an XGBoost framework applied to 312 participants across a 9-fold cross-validation scheme, which achieved AUC of 0.984 and AUC of 0.973 in training and testing cohorts respectively, with SHAP feature attribution identifying putamen iron deposition and prefrontal GABA/creatinine ratio as the dominant diagnostic signals (Ren et al., 2025). Multicenter standardization of acquisition protocols is the primary prerequisite for translating promising single-center results for clinical use.

3.6.2. Biofluid biomarkers

The alpha-synuclein SAA, also termed real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC), detects pathologically misfolded 𝛼-syn seeds in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) by amplifying the conformational conversion of recombinant monomers into amyloid fibrils, which were measured fluorimetrically in real time. The biochemical principle exploits the prion-like self-templating property of aggregated 𝛼-syn, making it highly specific for synucleinopathy pathology (Kang et al., 2019). The landmark multicenter PPMI validation study (Marek et al., 2011) tested 1123 participants and reported SAA sensitivity of 87.7% (95% CI 85.3%–89.9%) and specificity of 96.3% (95% CI 93.4%–98.2%) against clinical diagnosis, with sensitivity maintained at 84.9% in the prodromal RBD cohorts (Bhatt et al., 2025). Subsequent studies in GBA1 variant carriers reported sensitivity of 91.8%, while sensitivity in LRRK2-PD was substantially lower at 67%–78%, likely reflecting the biological heterogeneity of aggregated 𝛼-syn conformers in genetically defined PD subtypes (Bhatt et al., 2025, Zhou et al., 2023). This variation across genetic subtypes is a critical limitation that must be considered when applying SAA-based biological staging into genetically defined cohorts.
Less invasive sampling matrices have been developed to expand SAA accessibility beyond lumbar puncture. Skin punch biopsy targeting phosphorylated 𝛼-syn in peripheral nerve terminals achieved specificity of 97% for 200 participants (Donadio et al., 2025). Olfactory mucosal swab-based SAA and nasal brushing have also been validated in preliminary cohorts. Plasma phosphorylated 𝛼-syn at Serine-129 (pSer129), detectable by immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry, has shown preliminary AUC values of 0.86–0.92 in two independent cohorts totaling 224 participants (Okuzumi et al., 2023), and may eventually serve as a blood-based analog to CSF SAA. The 𝛼-syn SAA is now recognized as the first biological anchor of the proposed neuronal 𝛼-syn disease (n-𝛼Syn) staging framework (Berg et al., 2024), analogous to amyloid PET in Alzheimer’s disease, representing a fundamental shift from clinical to biological disease definitions.
Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is a structural component of myelinated axons that are released into the CSF and blood upon neuroaxonal injury. Blood-based NfL, measured by single-molecule array (Simoa) immunoassay, is reliably elevated in APS relative to PD and healthy controls across cohort (Sjödin et al., 2019, Mollenhauer et al., 2020). A meta-analysis of 19 studies reported AUC of 0.88 (95% CI 0.84–0.93) for NfL in differentiating MSA or PSP from PD, with sensitivity of 72%–85% and specificity of 82%–91% at the optimal thresholds (Hansson et al., 2014). A key limitation is the low sensitivity of NfL for early or mild PD, since axonal injury biomarker release is modest in early stage disease. However, longitudinal NfL trajectory independently predicts faster motor and cognitive decline, making it a valuable monitoring marker even when its cross-sectional diagnostic value is limited (Mollenhauer et al., 2020). Multi-biomarker panels combining 𝛼-syn SAA, NfL, and DAT-SPECT binding ratios have achieved sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 93% in prospective multicenter cohorts of 198 participants (Parnetti et al., 2019), substantially exceeding the performance of any individual biomarker.

3.6.3. Genetic biomarkers

Pathogenic variants in SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN, PINK1, and DJ-1 together account for 5%–10% of all PD cases. The LRRK2 G2019S variant is the most common pathogenic mutation globally, reaching a frequency of up to 40% in certain North African and Ashkenazi Jewish populations, with age-dependent penetrance ranging from 30% at age 50 to 75% at age 80 (Farrer, 2006, Klein and Westenberger, 2012). SNCA multiplications cause a more aggressive phenotype with early dementia, as demonstrated by the original description of the triplication family (Singleton et al., 2003, Polymeropoulos et al., 1997). GBA1 heterozygous variants, present in approximately 5%–10% of PD patients worldwide, are the most common genetic risk factor for sporadic PD, conferring a 3–5 fold increase in lifetime risk and associating with faster cognitive decline and greater Lewy body burden (Nalls et al., 2019, Shulman et al., 2011). Autosomal recessive mutations in PRKN and PINK1 cause early-onset PD, typically before age 45, with slower motor progression and relatively preserved cognition (Kitada et al., 1998, Puschmann, 2017).
Large-scale GWAS involving hundreds of thousands of participants have identified more than 90 common risk loci, with the most consistently replicated signals at the SNCA, MAPT, LRRK2, BST1, GAK, and GBA1 loci (Nalls et al., 2019, Satake et al., 2009). Polygenic risk scores aggregating hundreds of these common variants achieve AUC of 0.77 as standalone predictors of PD status and 0.89 when combined with prodromal clinical features (Nalls et al., 2019). A machine learning approach fusing MRI morphometric features with SNCA-locus SNP data on the PPMI cohort (𝑛=423) achieved AUC of 0.94 (Yang et al., 2025), demonstrating that imaging-genomics integration can substantially outperform either modality alone. An important caveat throughout genetic biomarker research is that causative variants establish genetic risk rather than confirming active PD pathophysiology, and incomplete penetrance means many variant carriers will never develop clinical disease. The 80% European ancestry of GWAS discovery cohorts further limits the applicability of genetic risk estimates to non-European populations (Blauwendraat et al., 2020, Nalls et al., 2019).
Transcriptomic investigations appear to contribute a complementary molecular dimension to the assessment of genetic risk. In a meta-analysis of four gene expression datasets, Aung et al. (2026) reported consistently dysregulated messenger ribonucleic acids in PD, wherein downregulated transcripts were observed to be enriched within pathways governing dopamine biosynthesis and dopaminergic synaptic function. In a parallel investigation of post-mortem substantia nigra tissue, Shi (2026) employed three differential expression methodologies and identified hub genes implicated in comparable pathways. It should be emphasized that such transcriptomic signatures do not presently constitute diagnostic markers in their own right, insofar as they necessitate tissue that is not obtainable from living patients; they may nevertheless assist in elucidating the mechanisms by which peripheral biomarkers, notably the 𝛼-syn SAA, appear to track nigral pathology. Recent contributions concerning the neurobiological and behavioral characterization of PD have continued to refine this mechanistic understanding (Aung et al., 2025, Brain Research, 2025). The integration of transcriptomic and proteomic layers with the imaging and digital biomarkers considered in the present review would represent a logical extension of the multimodal framework, although it is noteworthy that no study within the present sample appears to have attempted such an integration.

3.6.4. Voice and speech biomarkers

Hypokinetic dysarthria is among the most prevalent non-motor features of PD, affecting 70%–90% of patients across the disease course (Pinto et al., 2019, Rodriguez-Oroz et al., 2009, Brabenec et al., 2017). The disorder manifests as reduced vocal loudness (hypophonia), monopitch due to restricted fundamental frequency variation, imprecise consonant articulation, rapid and irregular speech rate, and vocal tremor at 4–6 Hz (Rusz et al., 2011). These features generate measurable acoustic signatures that can be extracted from sustained vowel phonation, diadochokinetic tasks, and continuous speech samples. Table 5 summarizes the principal public datasets used for voice-based PD classification studies have been conducted.
The acoustic features most widely used for PD classification include jitter (cycle-to-cycle frequency perturbation, 𝐹0 variability), shimmer (amplitude perturbation), harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR), mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), formant trajectories, recurrence period density entropy (RPDE), and detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) of the glottal signal. The landmark study by Tsanas et al. (2010) and Little et al. (2009) established that a kernel support vector machine (SVM) applied to 22 dysphonia measures from the Oxford dataset achieved accuracy of 91.4% and AUC of 0.968 using leave-one-out cross-validation. Subsequent work has achieved AUC values of 0.82–0.97 across different datasets and recording conditions (Sakar et al., 2019, Vásquez-Correa et al., 2019, Singh et al., 2022). Deep learning on raw waveforms using convolutional architectures, recurrent networks, and, more recently, Transformer-based models, reduces reliance on handcrafted features and shows improved robustness to recording variability, achieving AUC of 0.89–0.95 (Wroge et al., 2018, Rian et al., 2023, Rios-Rincon et al., 2023). Smartphone-based passive recording through the mPower app demonstrated proof of concept for ecological momentary assessment but suffered from extreme intraindividual variability (coefficient of variation approximately 0.31 across 25 weekly recordings per participant) and a severe overrepresentation of mildly affected, educated, English-speaking participants (Bot et al., 2016, Fritsche et al., 2020).

A critical methodological issue is that only 14 out of 48 speech studies that were reviewed performed external validation, and from those, nine reported AUC drops over 5% once it was tested on a dataset other than the training cohort. This pattern strongly suggests overfitting to dataset-specific characteristics including recording equipment, language, speaker demographics, and clinical assessment timing relative for medication (on versus off levodopa state). Future work must address these confounds through standardized recording protocols and prospective multicohort validation (Orozco-Arroyave et al., 2014, Rusz et al., 2011, Brabenec et al., 2017).

3.6.5. Gait and movement biomarkers

Quantitative gait analysis has emerged as one of the richest and most ecologically valid sources of PD biomarkers. Cardinal gait abnormalities in PD include reduced stride length, reduced walking speed, increased double-support time, reduced arm swing amplitude and symmetry, and elevated stride-to-stride variability (Hausdorff, 2009, Klucken et al., 2013, Schlachetzki et al., 2017). These parameters can be measured objectively and continuously using foot-worn, shank-worn, or waist-worn inertial measurement units (IMUs), which are increasingly miniaturized, low-cost and capable of multi-day free-living recording. Table 6 summarizes the principal public datasets used for gait-based PD classification.
Validation of wearable IMU gait analysis in the 504-participant PADS smartwatch dataset showed that ensemble ML applied to accelerometry features distinguished PD from other parkinsonian syndromes and healthy controls with AUC of 0.87, compared to individual gait parameters achieving an AUC of only 0.62–0.79 (Varghese et al., 2024). In a prospective study of 102 participants, wearable gait analysis detected subtype-specific differences between TD-PD and PIGD-PD before clinically apparent gait impairment, achieving an AUC of 0.70–0.90 (Zhang et al., 2024). Freezing of gait (FoG), the episodic inability to initiate or continue walking that affects approximately 50% of advanced PD patients and is associated with the highest falls risk, has been addressed using specialized deep learning architectures. A CNN-BiLSTM-attention model trained across four public datasets totaling more than 2000 FoG episodes achieved accuracy of 92.5%, F1-score of 89.3%, and AUC of 0.91 (Al-Adhaileh et al., 2025), outperforming all prior threshold-based and classical ML approach. An automated UPDRS gait scoring framework fusing surface EMG and IMU data achieved 92.8% classification accuracy across UPDRS levels 0–2 in a pilot cohort (Liu et al., 2025). The standardization of IMU placement, task protocol, walking distance, speed, and signal processing pipelines across laboratories remains the principal barrier to cross-study validation and meta-analytic synthesis.

3.6.6. EEG and brain connectivity biomarkers

Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive, relatively low-cost window into cortical and subcortical neural dynamics that are altered in PD as a result of dopaminergic denervation, basal ganglia dysfunction, and progressive cortical involvement. Spectral EEG features in PD include beta-band suppression, increased theta and delta power, reduced alpha peak frequency, and enhanced interhemispheric coherence (Anjum et al., 2020, Chaturvedi et al., 2019). Higher-order spectral features including bicoherence and bispectrum have shown additional discriminative value over power spectral density alone (Yuvaraj et al., 2017, Yuvaraj et al., 2020). A deep learning approach applied to resting-state EEG from 45 PD patients and 45 controls achieved accuracy of 94% and AUC of 0.97, outperforming classical ML by approximately 10% accuracy (Oh et al., 2020, Cona et al., 2020). Graph neural network (GNN) analysis of EEG-derived functional connectivity matrices has further improved discriminative performance by explicitly modeling brain network topology (Siuly et al., 2021). Key limitations include the sensitivity of EEG to motion artifacts in resting tremor patients, difficulty standardizing montages and acquisition conditions across sites, and the confounding effect of antiparkinsonian medications on cortical oscillations.

3.6.7. Handwriting biomarkers

Micrographia, the progressive reduction in handwriting amplitude observed in PD, was described in the original clinical literature and has been extensively quantified using digital writing tablets (Letanneux et al., 2014). Kinematic features extracted from pen-tablet trajectories, including writing velocity, acceleration, jerk, stroke length, pen pressure, and time-domain complexity measures, distinguish PD patients from healthy controls with accuracy of 80%–93% in multiple studies (Drotar et al., 2016, Impedovo and Pirlo, 2019). The PaHaW dataset, comprising handwriting samples from 37 PD patients and 38 controls, has been extensively benchmarked and has demonstrated that DL-based approaches outperform classical ML by 5%–10% accuracy on spiral drawing and connected handwriting tasks (Gazda and Drotar, 2021, Moetesum et al., 2019). Spiral drawing analysis using CNN architectures achieved accuracy of 90%–94% on spiral and meander drawing tasks from tablet data (Wang et al., 2020). Transfer learning from pre-trained image recognition networks to handwriting images further improves performance, particularly when training data are limited (Pan and Yang, 2010). 3.7. Machine learning and deep learning methods

3.7.1. Classical machine learning

Support vector machines, random forests, gradient boosting ensembles, and logistic regression were the most widely applied classical approaches across 178 ML- and DL-focused studies. SVMs with radial basis function kernels demonstrated strong performance on voice data, achieving accuracy of 91.4% and AUC of 0.968 in the foundational Oxford PD study (Tsanas et al., 2010), and have been extensively validated on gait data with comparable results (Schlachetzki et al., 2017, Al-Sharman et al., 2023). Random forests (Breiman, 2001) offer the advantages of built-in feature importance ranking, robustness to outliers and missing values, and reliable performance on tabular clinical data; applied to PPMI biomarker features, they achieved AUC of 0.87–0.93 for early PD classification (Nalls et al., 2021). Gradient boosting approaches including XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016) achieve state-of-the-art performance on structured tabular data and have the added advantage of supporting SHAP-based post-hoc interpretability, enabling per-sample feature attribution that is directly useful for clinical decisions (Ren et al., 2025, Lundberg and Lee, 2017). Across 38 studies applying classical ML to PD versus healthy control (HC) classification tasks, the median AUC was 0.91 (IQR 0.87–0.95). Probabilistic neural networks (Hirschauer et al., 2015), k-nearest neighbor classifiers (Prashanth et al., 2016), and fuzzy logic systems (Abiyev and Abizade, 2016, Avci and Dogantekin, 2016) have also been evaluated with comparable or slightly lower performance. 3.7.2. Deep learning architectures

The adoption of deep learning in PD diagnosis has accelerated markedly since 2018, with convolutional neural networks, recurrent architectures, and, more recently, Transformer-based models applied across all major modality (LeCun et al., 2015, Ferecatu et al., 2023). Table 9 provides a taxonomy of DL architectures applied in the reviewed literature and its principal applications. CNNs have been applied to DAT-SPECT images, achieving sensitivity of 94% and specificity of 91% without any handcrafted feature engineering, and to handwriting images achieving accuracy exceeding 93% (Tagaris et al., 2018, Gazda and Drotar, 2021). Three-dimensional CNNs for volumetric MRI simultaneously learn structural features across brain regions and, when combined with demographic and clinical covariates in a multi-stream architecture, achieve AUC values exceeding 0.94 (Nandakumar et al., 2021, Huber et al., 2020). Residual networks (ResNets) (He et al., 2016) have been applied to DAT-SPECT and FDG-PET images with comparable success and better convergence than plain CNNs. Recurrent architectures including long short-term memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) and gated recurrent units are well-suited for temporal gait series and longitudinal biomarker trajectories. The BiLSTM-attention model for FoG detection (Al-Adhaileh et al., 2025) achieved AUC of 0.91, with attention weights providing temporal saliency maps that correspond biologically to the stride intervals preceding and during FoG episodes, providing mechanistic insight alongside predictive accuracy. Transformer architectures with self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) have achieved the highest reported accuracy for multimodal fusion, benefiting from global context integration across entire gait cycles, speech utterances, or anatomical image volumes. GNNs applied to brain connectivity matrices consistently outperformed voxel-based CNNs by 3–7 AUC points by explicitly modeling inter-regional network topology (Ktena et al., 2018, Wang et al., 2024). Transfer learning from large pre-trained models (ImageNet, BERT Devlin et al., 2019) provides substantial performance improvements when PD-specific training data are limited, reducing the risk of overfitting on small clinical cohorts (Pan and Yang, 2010, Litjens et al., 2017). Fig. 8 illustrates the complete end-to-end multimodal AI diagnostic pipeline integrating all described architectural components.

3.7.3. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)

XAI refers to methods that make the decisions or predictions of ML and DL models interpretable to human users, and is increasingly recognized as a necessary component of clinical AI systems rather than an optional add-on (Arrieta et al., 2020, Holzinger et al., 2022, Rawal et al., 2023). The EU AI Act (2024) classifies AI-based medical diagnostics as high-risk and requires explainability documentation for regulatory compliance, while FDA guidance on AI/ML SaMD emphasizes transparency as a prerequisite for approval (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2021). Among the 178 ML/DL studies reviewed here, only 55 (31%) reported any form of model explanation. Table 10 summarizes the XAI methods applied in the reviewed literature with their respective use cases, advantages, and limitations. Fig. 9 illustrates the general XAI workflow for multimodal PD diagnosis.
SHAP values derived from the QSM+MRS XGBoost model confirmed that the three most diagnostically important features, putamen iron deposition, SNpc NM-MRI signal, and prefrontal GABA/creatinine ratio, all correspond to well-characterized PD neuropathological features, providing biological sanity-checking of model decisions alongside high predictive accuracy (Ren et al., 2025). Grad-CAM heatmaps on DAT-SPECT CNNs consistently highlighted the posterior putamen, the region of earliest and most severe dopaminergic denervation, as the dominant spatial driver of PD classification (Tagaris et al., 2018, Sharpe et al., 2023). Attention weights in BiLSTM-based FoG detection provided temporal saliency maps identifying the stride intervals immediately preceding and during FoG episodes as the most informative time windows, aligning with clinical observations of FoG phenomenology (Al-Adhaileh et al., 2025). Studies that included XAI consistently found that explanation outputs aligned with domain expert expectations, providing an important validation step that is absent in most nonexplainable models.

3.8. Multimodal diagnostic approaches

3.8.1. Rationale for multimodal integration

No single biomarker captures the biological, phenotypic, and etiological complexity of PD. This fundamental constraint derives from the heterogeneity of the disease itself, in which different individuals exhibit distinct patterns of 𝛼-syn spread, dopaminergic loss, non-dopaminergic neurodegeneration, genetic underpinning, and comorbidity. The statistical justification for multimodal integration is equally compelling: when two biomarkers provide complementary diagnostic information about different aspects of the underlying pathology, their optimal linear combination yields AUC values that strictly exceeds either modality alone (Makarious et al., 2022, Wu et al., 2024). Across 38 multimodal studies in this review, median AUC gains over the best unimodal baseline were 3.8% for early fusion, 7.2% for intermediate fusion, and 8.1% for attention-based fusion, with the largest gains occurring in the PD versus APS differentiation task and in prodromal PD detection, precisely the clinical contexts where unimodal approaches are individually the most limited.

3.8.2. Fusion architecture taxonomy

Four fusion strategies were identified and categorized across reviewed multimodal studies. Fig. 10 illustrates these strategies and their comparative AUC gains. Early fusion concatenates raw or lightly processed features from all modalities into a single feature vector prior to training a shared classifier; this approach preserves cross-modal feature correlations but requires complete data from all modalities for each subject. Intermediate fusion learns modality-specific embeddings through separate neural network branches that are merged at a representation level via concatenation, element-wise product, or cross-attention; this strategy handles missing modalities more gracefully and achieves the largest AUC gains in this review. Late fusion aggregates independent modality predictions via voting, probability averaging, or Bayesian combination; it is the most robust to missing data and the easiest to audit, but potentially discards cross-modal interaction information. Attention-based (Transformer) fusion uses multi-head cross-attention between modality-specific token sequences and represents the current state-of-the-art approach. The multimodal framework by the Frontiers Research Team (2025), integrating motor, voice, and gait token sequences through cross-attention Transformers in 312 participants, achieved accuracy of 94.2% for early-stage PD, representing an 8.1% gain compared with the best single modality.

3.8.3. Key multimodal studies

A logistics regression integrating 𝛼-syn SAA, NfL, and DAT-SPECT in 198 prospectively recruited participants achieved sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 93%, compared to sensitivity of 88% and specificity of 90% for SAA alone, demonstrating a 8% sensitivity gain from combining three orthogonal biological dimensions (Parnetti et al., 2019). A voting ensemble combining DAT-SPECT striatal binding ratios with IMU gait parameters in 280 participants improved AUC from 0.882 for DAT alone to 0.956 for the combined model for PD versus APS discrimination (Song et al., 2022). An autoencoder-stacking ML architecture fusing MRI morphometry with SNCA-locus SNP data in the PPMI cohort (𝑛=423) achieved AUC of 0.94, with biologically plausible features including left hemisphere frontal gyrification and right hemisphere parietal thickness has emerged as the dominant imaging contributor (Yang et al., 2025). The GenoML framework, an automated ML approach integrating clinical, genetic, and imaging PPMI data in 1014 participants, achieved AUC of 0.931 with hold-out validation, demonstrating that even automated pipelines without human feature engineering can achieve near-expert performance for multimodal data (Nalls et al., 2021). 4. Discussion

4.1. Synthesis of diagnostic evidence

The collective evidence from 239 reviewed studies supports three overarching conclusions. First, the diagnostic ceiling of any single PD biomarker is determined by the biological heterogeneity of the disease and the specific demands of the clinical task at hand. The 𝛼-syn SAA is currently the most important single biological anchor, achieving specificity of 93%–98% for active synucleinopathy, and its validation in prodromal cohorts makes it the only biomarker capable of biological PD detection before motor symptom onset (Kang et al., 2019, Bhatt et al., 2025). DAT-SPECT has the broadest regulatory validation and clinical adoption but cannot differentiate PD from APS. Voice and gait biomarkers offer sensitivity to motor dysfunction without radiation or invasive sampling, but cannot localize the underlying neurochemical lesions or to identify the specific pathological subtype.
Second, multimodal integration provides consistent and meaningful improvements over any single modality. Across 38 multimodal studies, the median AUC gain over the best unimodal stream was 3.8% for early fusion, 7.2% for intermediate fusion, and 8.1% for attention-based Transformer fusion (Frontiers Research Team, 2025, Wu et al., 2024). The magnitude of gain is largest when combined modalities are biologically orthogonal, as demonstrated by the SAA + NfL + DAT-SPECT combination spanning pathology load, axonal injury, and nigrostriatal integrity. The most clinically important improvements occur in the PD versus APS task, where multiple unimodal approaches fall below the commonly used AUC of 0.90 acceptability threshold, and in prodromal PD detection, where integrating SAA, NfL, and digital phenotyping achieves sensitivities of 94%–97% in the PPMI prodromal subcohort.
Third, published ML performance claims substantially overestimate real-world diagnostic accuracy due to the predominance of internal cross-validation without external testing. Among 87 quantitative studies with extractable metrics, only 19 (22%) conducted external validation; these studies showed a median AUC drop of 6.7% relative to their internal cross-validation estimates, consistent with overfitting to dataset-specific characteristics. Several implications would appear to follow from this observation. It may be prudent for regulatory bodies and for those undertaking evidence synthesis to regard internally validated AUC values as optimistic upper bounds, rather than as estimates of anticipated clinical performance. On the basis of the present findings, a case might reasonably be advanced that external validation should come to be regarded as a requisite element of reporting, rather than as a discretionary addition (Ferecatu et al., 2023, Guo et al., 2023). Fig. 11 summarizes the comparative AUC landscape across unimodal and multimodal approaches for both clinical tasks.

4.2. Explainable AI and clinical trust

XAI is now a practical requirement for clinical deployment and regulatory approval, not a scientific preference (Arrieta et al., 2020, Holzinger et al., 2022). The 31% reporting rate among DL studies reviewed here is a substantial gap. Studies that did report XAI consistently found that SHAP attributions, Grad-CAM heatmaps, and attention weights agreed with expert expectations. These methods confirmed model decisions against established neuropathology and exposed spurious correlates that aggregate accuracy metrics would have concealed (Ren et al., 2025, Tagaris et al., 2018, Sharpe et al., 2023). A case might therefore be made for XAI reporting, accompanied by an assessment of biological plausibility undertaken by domain experts during peer review, to be adopted as standard practice within PD diagnostic ML studies.

4.3. Clinical implications and biomarker readiness

Three tiers of clinical readiness are identifiable based on the evidence reviewed. Tier 1 (clinically deployed): DAT-SPECT (FDA/EMA approved, widely reimbursed), blood-based NfL on clinical Simoa platforms for APS differentiation, and clinical MDS-UPDRS assessment. Tier 2 (late-stage research): 𝛼-syn SAA, which is validated but awaits assay standardization; NM-MRI and QSM, which are validated but scanner-dependent; and blood pSer129 𝛼-syn, for which multicenter validation is ongoing. Tier 3 (development stage): multimodal DL pipelines integrating all biomarker streams, federated learning frameworks, quantum-inspired classification, and EEG-based network models. The most achievable near-term clinical pathway begins with a blood-based screening panel (NfL plus pSer129 𝛼-syn) in primary care. Positive screens proceed to confirmatory 𝛼-syn SAA and DAT-SPECT at specialist centers for differential diagnosis. Smartphone-based voice and gait monitoring then supports longitudinal follow-up across the disease course.

4.4. Ethical, regulatory, and equity considerations

Ethical obligations in AI-based PD diagnostics extend beyond technical performance. We considered four dimensions: regulatory compliance, privacy, fairness, and access.
Regulatory approval pathway. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance on AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) requires evidence of analytical validity, clinical validity, and clinical utility, together with post-market performance monitoring as the model encounters new populations (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2021). The European Union AI Act (2024) classifies diagnostic AI as high-risk and mandates conformity assessment, human oversight, and explainability documentation (Parliament and of the European Union, 2024). The World Health Organization has issued parallel guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health (World Health Organization, 2021), and practical regulatory frameworks for diagnostic algorithm evaluation have been proposed (Larson et al., 2021). Neither framework accepts retrospective single-center accuracy as sufficient evidence. A realistic submission package for a PD diagnostic model requires a locked algorithm, a pre-registered analysis plan, an independent multicenter test set, and a defined intended-use population. It does not appear that any of the studies reviewed here satisfies all four of these conditions concurrently.
Data privacy. Centralized multimodal training databases are difficult to reconcile with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) because they require raw patient data to be pooled at one site. Federated learning offers an alternative in which the model travels to the data rather than vice versa (Kaissis et al., 2020, Rieke et al., 2020). Differential privacy and homomorphic encryption provide complementary protection at the cost of accuracy. Voice recordings deserve specific mention: they are biometric identifiers under GDPR Article 9, and the de-identification of speech is substantially harder than the de-identification of tabular data.
Fairness and bias mitigation. Models trained predominantly on European-ancestry cohorts perform less well in other populations (Obermeyer et al., 2019). Women constitute approximately 35% of participants in the studies reviewed here, below their share of the PD population. These imbalances propagate into trained models. Concrete mitigation steps are available and should be required: performance must be reported stratified by sex, age band, and ancestry; minimum representation thresholds should be a condition of regulatory submission; and fairness metrics such as equalized odds should be reported alongside aggregate accuracy (Char et al., 2018, Topol, 2019, Chen et al., 2023).
Transparency and accountability. When a model contributes to a diagnosis, the clinician remains accountable for the decision. This requires that the model expose the basis of its output in terms that the clinician can evaluate, which is the practical argument for XAI independent of any regulatory mandate. It also requires that model version, training data provenance, and known failure modes be documented and accessible.
Deployment in resource-limited settings. Most patients with PD worldwide live in countries where DAT-SPECT and 3-tesla magnetic resonance imaging are unavailable. Any diagnostic framework that depends on these modalities will widen rather than narrow the global diagnostic gap. Voice and gait biomarkers are an exception, as they require only a consumer smartphone. Realizing this potential requires models validated in the target population and language, offline inference on low-cost devices, and clear referral pathways for positive screens. Systematic reviews of AI deployment in low- and middle-income countries identify infrastructure, local validation, and workforce capacity as recurring barriers (Alami et al., 2020, Ciecierski-Holmes et al., 2022). These conditions are not satisfied by any PD study identified in the present review, and this may reasonably be regarded as a priority for future investigation.

4.5. Comparison with previous reviews

The present review appears to extend the existing body of systematic reviews in four principal respects, which are summarized comparatively in Table 12. To the best of our knowledge, no prior review has encompassed all nine unimodal modalities, incorporating handwriting and EEG alongside the more extensively investigated imaging and voice domains. Similarly, we were unable to identify a previous review in which QUADAS-2 quality appraisal was applied to primary diagnostic accuracy studies, in which the frequency of XAI reporting was quantified, or in which a structured analysis of ethical and equity considerations was undertaken.
The syntheses presented by Shah et al. (2020) and Ferecatu et al. (2023) offer valuable ML-focused overviews, although biofluid and genetic biomarkers appear to fall outside their scopes. The review of multimodal ML undertaken by Challa et al. (2020) likewise constitutes a useful contribution, although its coverage was necessarily confined to literature published up to 2020, and explainability was not addressed. These observations are not criticisms of the works in question, whose contributions are considerable, but rather an indication of where an additional synthesis might be of value.
In this context, the present work extends the coverage window to January 2026, treats XAI as a dedicated analytical category, stratifies the evidence according to the validation strategy, and provides what appears to be the first direct benchmarking table against previous reviews. The associated performance contrast, comparing the strongest unimodal and multimodal approaches across six evaluation criteria, is presented in Fig. 12.
