4.6. Limitations of the evidence and this review

The evidence base for AI-based PD diagnosis is characterized by several systemic limitations that constrain the confidence of conclusions drawn from this study. Publication bias is inherent to any systematic literature review: studies reporting high diagnostic accuracy are substantially more likely to be published and indexed in the databases searched here than null or negative results, potentially inflating the median performance estimates across the field. The language restriction to English publications may exclude important contributions from non-English-speaking research groups, particularly from Japan, South Korea, China, and French-speaking African countries, where PD epidemiology and genetic architecture differ meaningfully from Western cohorts. Preprint servers including bioRxiv and medRxiv, where a growing fraction of recent ML work appears first, were not systematically searched.
The substantial heterogeneity in participant populations, reference standards (98% of included studies used clinical rather than neuropathological diagnosis), recording conditions, preprocessing pipelines, and performance metric reporting precluded formal Meta-analytic pooling of diagnostic accuracy estimates. The performance ranges presented in Table 7, Table 8, Table 9, Table 10, Table 11 represent the envelope of evidence from included studies, not pooled estimates with formal confidence intervals. QUADAS-2 assessment identified high patient selection bias in 31% and high reference standard bias in 24% of included primary studies; performance statistics from these high-risk studies should be interpreted conservatively, as potential overestimates of true diagnostic accuracy. Regarding the boundaries of this review, therapeutic monitoring, disease progression tracking, and treatment response biomarkers were not systematically evaluated, as these represent distinct clinical questions warranting a separate review.
Two further limitations pertaining to the conduct of the review warrant acknowledgment. First, as noted in Section 2, the review was not prospectively registered with the PROSPERO database. Although efforts were made to mitigate the attendant risk, insofar as the protocol elements were documented in writing prior to the commencement of screening and no post-hoc modifications were made to the eligibility criteria, it must be conceded that prospective registration would have afforded a more robust safeguard against selective reporting. Second, gray literature, doctoral dissertations, and preprint repositories were not systematically searched. Given that an increasing proportion of methodological work in this field appears first on preprint servers, the coverage of the most recent developments may be subject to some degree of lag. Both limitations are acknowledged here, and their correction would be advisable in any subsequent updates of this review.

5. Conclusions and future directions

PD diagnosis is being reshaped by the convergence of molecular biomarker science, digital phenotyping, and AI-based analytics. This review of 239 studies supports four conclusions. Multimodal integration guided by ML and DL frameworks, particularly attention-based transformer fusion, outperforms any single modality, with AUC gains up to 8% and the largest improvements in early-stage detection and APS differentiation. The 𝛼-syn SAA has become the most important biological anchor, with sensitivity above 87% in prodromal cohorts. Voice and gait biomarkers offer the most realistic path to low-cost, globally accessible screening. There are compelling grounds, both scientific and regulatory, for XAI to be regarded as a standard component of model development.
The fifth observation, which follows from the analysis presented in Section 3.3, invites a more cautious appraisal. The evidence base appears to be dominated by retrospective, single-center investigations that employ internal validation. External validation was reported in only 22% of studies, recruitment extended beyond three centers in only 2.5%, and we were unable to identify any randomized trial in which an AI-based diagnostic tool had been evaluated with respect to its effect on patient management or clinical outcomes. Based on these findings, it might tentatively be suggested that the principal impediment to clinical adoption no longer resides in model architecture but rather in the relative scarcity of prospective multicenter evidence.

5.1. Clinical translation: Regulatory approval, workflow integration, and deployment

Moving from published accuracy to bedside use requires three things that current studies do not provide.
Regulatory approval. A viable FDA or European Union submission requires a locked algorithm, a pre-specified analysis plan, an independent multicenter test set drawn from the intended-use population, and documentation of explainability (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2021, Arrieta et al., 2020). We recommend that model developers design validation studies to meet these requirements from the outset rather than retrofitting existing models. The alpha-synuclein SAA offers a useful precedent: its path toward clinical acceptance followed multicenter validation in a predefined cohort with a locked assay protocol (Kang et al., 2019, Marek et al., 2011).
Workflow integration. A diagnostic model is useful only if it fits the clinical encounter. For a primary care setting, this means a result available within the consultation, an interface that requires no specialist training, and an output expressed as a referral decision rather than a probability. For a movement disorder clinic, this means integration with the electronic health record and interoperability with existing imaging and laboratory systems. We were unable to identify any study within the present sample in which workflow testing, clinician time burden, or usability evaluation had been reported. There would appear to be merit in these becoming established reporting items.
Real-world deployment and monitoring. Model performance degrades as populations, scanners, and clinical practices change. Post-deployment monitoring with predefined performance thresholds and retraining triggers is a regulatory expectation under the FDA SaMD framework and should be planned before deployment, not after (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2021, Vokinger et al., 2021).

5.2. Standardization, reporting, and reproducibility

Cross-study comparability is currently limited by the absence of shared standards, which is a tractable problem.
Data acquisition protocols. We recommend that learned societies and regulatory bodies jointly develop minimum acquisition standards: for voice, a specified phonation task, recording device class, sampling rate, and ambient noise ceiling; for gait, specified sensor placement, walking task, and distance; and for magnetic resonance imaging, specified field strength and sequence parameters. Without these, external validation will continue to fail for reasons unrelated to underlying biology.
Reporting guidelines. Existing instruments are adequate and need to be applied. STARD 2015 for diagnostic accuracy (Bossuyt et al., 2015), TRIPOD+AI for prediction model reporting (Collins et al., 2024), and CLAIM for medical imaging AI (Mongan et al., 2020) together cover these requirements. We recommend that journals require the completion of the relevant checklist as a condition of review.
Benchmark datasets and code. Public benchmark datasets with held-out test partitions, along with published training codes and model weights, allow for direct comparison of architectures on identical data. The PPMI (Marek et al., 2011) and mPower (Bot et al., 2016) resources provide a foundation, but neither offers a standardized, permanently held-out evaluation partition.

5.3. Longitudinal prediction, progression monitoring, and personalized medicine

Almost all studies reviewed here address a single question: does this person have PD at this moment. The clinically important questions are different and longitudinal.
Conversion prediction in prodromal cohorts. For a person with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder, the question is not whether they have PD but when they will convert and how quickly they will convert. Models that predict the time to conversion, rather than the current status, would directly serve neuroprotective trial enrollment. Work on motor progression prediction provides a template (Latourelle et al., 2017), and serum-based progression models have been reported (Ahmadi Rastegar et al., 2019), but this requires longitudinal cohorts with repeated multimodal sampling, and the data infrastructure largely does not yet exist in this regard.
Progression monitoring. Wearable and smartphone biomarkers are well suited for continuous monitoring, as they can be collected at high frequency at home at negligible cost. Their most valuable application may therefore not be diagnosis, where a single expert assessment is often sufficient, but progression tracking, where clinical assessment is expensive and infrequent.
Personalized therapeutic matching. Biological subtyping through 𝛼-syn SAA, genetic status, and imaging phenotype makes it possible in principle to match patients to mechanism-specific therapies, such as GBA1- or LRRK2-targeted agents. Data-driven subtyping from longitudinal clinical records (Zhang et al., 2019) and radiomics-based progression clustering (Salmanpour et al., 2022) demonstrate that this is feasible. Diagnostic models that output subtype rather than a binary label would support this directly, and we recommend that future multimodal models be trained and evaluated on subtype classification alongside diagnosis.
Multimodal longitudinal architectures. Recurrent and transformer models are naturally suited to irregularly sampled longitudinal data but have been applied to PD almost exclusively in cross-sectional settings. Extending them to trajectory modeling with explicit handling of missing visits and modalities is a clear methodological opportunity.

5.4. Research agenda

Several priorities follow from the evidence reviewed in this study: Biologically staged, personalized diagnosis should be the organizing framework, with the n-𝛼Syn staging proposal (Berg et al., 2024) providing a scaffold for pre-symptomatic research and trial enrollment. This scaffold should be prospectively validated in diverse longitudinally followed cohorts with neuropathological confirmation, where applicable. Blood-based multianalyte panels combining plasma pSer129 𝛼-syn, NfL, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and phosphorylated tau should be validated in multicenter cohorts of at least 1000 participants with adequate ethnic diversity. Flexible, missing-data-robust multimodal architectures, specifically masked transformer models and generative imputation networks, are needed because complete multimodal data are rarely available for any patient. International standardization of voice and gait acquisition protocols is a prerequisite for meaningful cross-site validations. Federated continual learning infrastructure (Kaissis et al., 2020, Rieke et al., 2020) enables privacy-preserving distributed training across geographically diverse sites. An equity-first cohort design, with minimum representation thresholds for non-European ancestries, women, and low-income populations, is necessary to prevent AI tools from amplifying existing health disparities (Obermeyer et al., 2019, Char et al., 2018). XAI as a mandatory reporting standard, with biological plausibility evaluated during peer review, will support regulatory approval and appropriate clinical reliance (Arrieta et al., 2020, Sharpe et al., 2023).
The scientific and technological foundations appear to be largely established. The tasks that remain are, in the main, translational in nature, encompassing protocol standardization, equitable data collection, prospective multicenter validation, and the development of appropriate regulatory science. Fig. 13 traces the parallel advances in biomarker science and AI methodology across the review window and may assist in situating the present position of the field within its broader historical context.
